# Permanent public health authority (`public_health_board`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by census_vital_registration, quarantine, epidemiology_mapping, probability_statistics
- Core idea: A standing office with legal powers, a budget and its own staff that records every death by cause and place, receives compulsory reports of suspect cases from physicians, inspects food, water, markets and lodging houses, isolates the sick, controls travel in epidemics and keeps streets and wells clean. Its strength is routine: deaths are counted every week whether or not there is an epidemic, so a rise is seen within days. Give it authority over all ranks and over the clergy's processions, and pay those it shuts in, or cases will be hidden.
- Pitfalls:
  - A committee formed only when plague has already arrived acts too late and dissolves afterwards
  - Powers without compensation: merchants and families conceal cases if isolation means ruin and starvation
  - Records that do not note cause and parish in a consistent way cannot show where an outbreak starts
  - Acting on miasma theory helps by accident (cleaning, burning bedding) but also wastes effort on perfumes and bonfires and on killing cats and dogs, which removes the rats' enemies
  - Challenging religious gatherings in an epidemic without the bishop's backing provokes riot
- History: rome: Republic and Empire – aediles oversee markets, streets and water; 11 BC a permanent water board (curatores aquarum); china: 1076 – the Song state founds public pharmacies and later relief clinics and paupers' hospitals; epidemic measures remain ad hoc; islamic: from 9th c. – the muhtasib inspects food, markets, baths, street cleanliness and medical practitioners (hisba manuals); no plague magistracy; europe: 1348 – Venice and Florence appoint temporary plague committees; c. 1450 Milan has a permanent health office with death registers from 1452; 1486 Venice's Provveditori alla Sanità; 1527 Florence makes its board permanent; 1848 English General Board of Health
- Read:
  - Carlo M. Cipolla, Public Health and the Medical Profession in the Renaissance (1976)
  - Carlo M. Cipolla, Fighting the Plague in Seventeenth-Century Italy (1981)
